\paragraphRuns. Each configuration of attacker, MTD and deployment interval in Table 1 is run on the same 1 000 seeds, the number recommended for randomised algorithms .
The 408 000 runs of Sections 1 and 1 took about 29 hours, seven at a time, on a laptop with an Intel Core i7-1360P processor, in Python 3.11 under Ubuntu 22.04.
Every metric at every configuration, with its interval, is published with the experiment scripts.
A component's effect is x on NCR, the APT attacker model with it minus without it.
The effect is negligible when its interval lies wholly inside x, not negligible when it lies wholly outside, and inconclusive when it crosses x .
The unmapped tactics include Collection, Exfiltration and Impact, the tactics of actions on objectives.
The baseline attacker's runs share one opening over their first \prelimfour steps, the order of its fixed procedure (Section 1).
All but \prelimtwo of its 1 000 runs then branch once, into brute force or scan neighbours, before enumerating a host again.

The baseline attacker's attack rate is \prelim1.709 attack actions per minute, against \prelim0.680 to \prelim1.228 for the attack profiles, and its attack confidentiality \prelim82.2 %, against \prelim89.4 to \prelim98.1 %.
The baseline attacker's MTTC, \prelim9 100 s, is just shorter than the attack profiles', \prelim9 700 to \prelim11 300 s.
Under every service-layer mechanism, attack actions blocked per MTD deployment is \prelim0.95 against \prelim0.15, and under user shuffle \prelim0.07 against \prelim0.01.
Under every other MTD mechanism, the APT attacker model loses \prelim26 s or less.

The first deployment disrupts the baseline attacker while it exploits its first exposed endpoint, and its procedure sends it straight back to that endpoint, keeping the progress it made there (Section 1).

At every deployment interval, rank 1 against the APT attacker model holds only host-layer mechanisms, and rank 1 against the baseline attacker only service-layer mechanisms (Table 1). x between the two attackers' NCR reductions is \prelim0.01 (\prelimx, \prelim0.05) at 200 s, and lies between \prelimx and \prelim0.25 at every deployment interval.

At 50 to 200 s, the deployment intervals the earlier MTDSim studies ran, the four attack profiles' NCR reductions differ from one another less than the baseline attacker's NCR reduction differs from the nearest attack profile's, under every MTD mechanism and deployment strategy (Figure 1).
Of the four attack profiles, x has the NCR reduction furthest from the baseline attacker's at \prelim500 and \prelim1 000 s, under the host-layer mechanisms and service diversity.
Under service diversity, the baseline attacker's NCR reduction is above all four, and x's is the lowest (panel f).

With no MTD, its NCR is 0.171 with the attack profiles and 0.189 without, a x of x. Under the MTD mechanisms and deployment strategies, the effect is not negligible in 29 of the 60 configurations, negligible in seven and inconclusive in 24 (Table 1).
With no MTD, the APT attacker model compromises more with the attack profiles than with any of the ten, by an effect on NCR that is not negligible, a x of 0.25 to 1.47 (Table 1).

After a failed Initial Access (the example of Section 1), the APT attacker model goes back to Reconnaissance in 0.76 to 0.83 of cases in x, x and x with the failure matrix, and in 0.08 to 0.10 without.
Section 1 scores the APT attacker model on the eight properties of Section 1, beside the three MTD attacker models scored there, and answers 1 and 1.

Collection, Exfiltration and Impact, the tactics of actions on objectives, are unmapped, because MTDSim's six attack actions only find and compromise hosts (Section 1), so the APT attacker model steals no data and impedes no system.
On choice of attack strategy, the attack profiles' 1 000 runs have 179 to 947 distinct openings over eight steps, and the baseline attacker's 3 (Figure 1(b)).

In each run, the Petri net picks the next tactic at random, in proportion to the edge weights (Equations 1 and 1), whereas the baseline attacker's procedure fixes the order of its attack actions (Figure 1).

On detection avoidance, the attack profiles have a lower attack rate than the baseline attacker, 0.68 to 1.23 attack actions per minute against 1.71, and a higher attack confidentiality, 89 to 98 % against 82 % (Table 1).

With the baseline attacker's times in place of its tactic durations, it takes 2.18 to 4.59 attack actions per minute, more than the baseline attacker, and its attack confidentiality falls to 32 to 56 %, below the baseline attacker's (Appendix 1).
Stealth and Defense Impairment, the tactics for avoiding detection, are unmapped, so in MTDSim its detection avoidance comes only from its tactic durations.

On adaptivity, the APT attacker model loses time mainly to the host layer, 242 to 324 s per deployment, where the baseline attacker's time lost is at or below zero; the baseline attacker loses time only to service diversity, 493 s per deployment, where the APT attacker model loses 60 s (Figure 1(b)).
The APT attacker model's tactic durations keep it mostly in unmapped tactics, which run no attack action (Section 1), and in Command and Control, which runs scan neighbours.
Consistent with this, attack actions blocked per MTD deployment under every service-layer mechanism is 0.15 for the APT attacker model, against 0.95 for the baseline attacker (Figure 1(a)).
All four attacker models lack cost--benefit reasoning, learning and deployment-strategy awareness.

In answer to 1, the APT attacker model executes the order of its tactics inside an existing simulator, MTDSim, as a Petri net that chooses its next tactic at runtime, mapping eight of the 15 tactics onto MTDSim's six attack actions (Section 1).
Two of those parts, the tactic durations and the failure matrix, fill what the threat reports do not record.
Three of them are Collection, Exfiltration and Impact, the tactics of actions on objectives, so objective-specific behaviour is in part.
MTDSim has no IDS, so the APT attacker model avoids detection only by proxy, through its tactic durations, and detection avoidance is in part.
On MTD modelling approaches, MTDShield reduces the baseline attacker's NCR more than the random deployment strategy does, but the APT attacker model's less, at every deployment interval.
Tay tested MTDShield in its training environment, against the baseline attacker, and compared it with no MTD .

An MTD evaluation should therefore test a learned deployment strategy against an attacker model other than the one it was trained against, beside the random deployment strategy over the same MTD mechanisms, which shows what the learning adds.
On effectiveness metrics, the two attackers rank the MTD mechanisms and deployment strategies differently, at every deployment interval.
Service diversity, for example, reduces the baseline attacker's NCR by 92 % and the APT attacker model's by 36 %, on the same networks (Table 1).

An MTD evaluation weighs the cost of MTD, such as system performance overhead and quality of service (Table 1), against the effectiveness of MTD. For a given MTD mechanism, the cost grows with how often it deploys, and how often it must deploy for a given NCR reduction depends on the attacker model.
Section 1 found that simulation, the dominant evaluation method, models specific attack behaviours flexibly but that its results do not transfer directly to a real network .
To mitigate this threat, we ablated the attack profiles, the failure matrix and the vulnerability memory one at a time, which rules out each as a cause of the host layer's lead (Section 1).
Only the APT attacker model has unmapped tactics, and at 200 s MTDShield chose to deploy nothing in 29 % of its decisions against it and 23 % against the baseline attacker, in 100 runs (Appendix 1).
NCR reduction can therefore credit an MTD mechanism that helps the baseline attacker reach a target host, because more of its runs then end early, with fewer hosts compromised.
To mitigate this threat, we also computed ASP reduction, and it orders the two layers as NCR reduction does, for both attackers, at every deployment interval (Table 1).
11 The APT attacker model only partially represents the likelihood, timing and response to failure of an APT attacker's steps, because attack flows record only their order.
Nor did we read the attacker models' code, which may behave differently from their papers, so the threat remains.
The ablations are weaker evidence, as they compare many cells without correction, so some may cross Cohen's threshold for a negligible effect, x, by chance.
In MTDSim, an IP shuffle costs the attacker the host it was on, but a real APT may keep that host through Command and Control.
They record only successful incidents worth writing about (Section 1), to the detail their threat reports give, and not all by APT groups (Section 1).
At every deployment interval, the host layer reduces the APT attacker model's NCR most, and the service layer reduces the baseline attacker's NCR most.
The first contribution is an APT attacker model that any study using MTDSim can run in place of the baseline attacker, answering 1 and 1.

Threat reports record the order of an attack's tactics, but not how long each took or what followed a failure, so the APT attacker model's timing and response to failure, where MTD disrupts it, rest on our judgement.

In MTDSim, the APT attacker model uses a Petri net to choose its next tactic at runtime, and maps each tactic onto one of the baseline attacker's six attack actions, none of which models actions on objectives.
In MTDSim, the most effective MTD mechanism depends on the attacker model.
The APT attacker model could then carry out actions on objectives, the part of objective-specific behaviour it lacks (Table 1).
The APT attacker model could then be tested on choosing techniques an IDS does not flag, the part of detection avoidance it lacks (Table 1).
